kp.k: SRA authorises its first purely AI-based regulated law firm
kp.d: In its 06 May 2025 news release, the SRA announces the authorisation of Garfield.Law Ltd to provide regulated legal services in England and Wales. It distinguishes this development from existing firms' use of AI for back-office and public-facing services; the first-of-its-kind claim concerns firms authorised by the SRA.
qs: While many firms are already using AI to support and deliver a range of back-office and public-facing services, Garfield.Law Ltd is the first purely AI-based firm we have authorised to provide regulated legal services in England and Wales.

kp.k: AI litigation assistant targets small-claims debt recovery
kp.d: The service is described as assisting small and medium sized businesses, law firms and other firms with recovering unpaid debts, guiding users through the small claims court process up to trial. This is a specified legal-service offering rather than a claim that AI can handle all litigation.
qs: the use of an AI-powered litigation assistant to help them recover unpaid debts, guiding them through the small claims court process up to trial.

kp.k: Authorisation requires quality, confidentiality and conflict safeguards
kp.d: The SRA reports engaging with Garfield.Law's owners before authorisation to assure itself that an AI-delivered service could meet its rules. Its review sought reassurance about processes for quality-checking work, protecting confidential client information and safeguarding against conflicts of interests; the release does not report measured service-quality results.
qs: Before authorising Garfield.Law, we engaged with the owners to consider the firm's processes and assure ourselves that our rules can be met by an AI service.
For instance, we have sought reassurance that there are appropriate processes in place to quality-check work, keep client information confidential, and safeguard against conflicts of interests.

kp.k: Case-law restrictions and client approval limit AI autonomy
kp.d: The SRA identifies proposing relevant case law as a high-risk area for large language models and says Garfield's system cannot do so. It also specifies client approval before every step, supervision and monitoring, and greater oversight of claims during the initial launch phase. These are reported risk controls, not evidence of an absence of hallucinations.
qs: We have also checked the firm is managing the risk of 'AI hallucinations.'
The system will not be able to propose relevant case law, which is a high-risk area for large language model machine learning.
Garfield is not autonomous and will only take a step where the client has approved it, and furthermore there are supervision and monitoring processes in place.
This includes greater oversight of claims in the initial launch phase, so that issues or risks can be identified.

kp.k: Solicitors retain accountability for AI outputs and failures
kp.d: The SRA states that named regulated solicitors remain ultimately accountable for professional standards, all system outputs and anything that goes wrong. It also notes that all regulated law firms must maintain a minimum level of insurance to protect clients. AI delivery therefore does not remove these stated professional responsibilities and protections.
qs: Under our rules, named regulated solicitors will still ultimately be accountable for the firm delivering high professional standards.
This means they will also be responsible for all the system outputs and for anything that goes wrong.
All regulated law firms must also have a minimum level of insurance in place to protect clients.

kp.k: Access and affordability benefits remain conditional expectations
kp.d: The SRA supports new service models for their potential to improve quality, speed and affordability, while requiring undiluted consumer protections. Chief Executive Paul Philip links responsible AI adoption to unmet legal-service needs among people and small businesses. These statements express anticipated public benefits rather than demonstrated outcomes or quantified savings.
qs: AI-driven legal services could deliver better, quicker and more affordable legal services.
With so many people and small businesses struggling to access legal services, we cannot afford to pull up the drawbridge on innovations that could have big public benefits.
Responsible use of AI by law firms could improve legal services, while making them easier to access and more affordable.

kp.k: SRA anticipates further AI firms and continued monitoring
kp.d: Philip characterises AI-driven firms' risks as novel and predicts that Garfield.Law is likely to be followed by further entrants. He commits the SRA to closely monitoring the model's progress to manage risks and realise consumer benefits; the release gives no numerical forecast or timetable for further authorisations.
qs: Any new law firm comes with potential risks, but the risks around an AI-driven law firm are novel.
As this is likely to be the first of many AI-driven law firms, we will be monitoring progress of this new model closely, so we can both manage the risks and realise the benefits to consumers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The SRA reports authorising its first purely AI-based regulated law firm, offering assistance with debt recovery through the small claims process.
pts.d: The SRA identifies Garfield.Law Ltd as the first purely AI-based firm it has authorised in England and Wales, distinguishing this model from existing firms' use of AI for support and service delivery. Its described service is an AI-powered litigation assistant for unpaid debts, guiding clients through the small claims court process up to trial.

pts.k: The SRA predicts potential improvements in quality, speed, affordability and access; its chief executive anticipates further AI-driven law firms.
pts.d: The SRA presents these benefits as possibilities rather than measured outcomes. Paul Philip, SRA Chief Executive, specifically links responsible AI use to improved access and affordability for people and small businesses struggling to obtain legal services. He describes Garfield as likely to be the first of many AI-driven law firms.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on the SRA's authorisation decision and review of Garfield's safeguards, not quantitative evidence of service improvements.
pts.d: The concrete example is an actual regulatory authorisation announced by the SRA. The regulator reports engaging with the owners and checking arrangements for quality control, confidentiality, conflicts and hallucination risk. The document supplies no performance benchmarks, cost comparisons, client outcomes or adoption data to substantiate the predicted benefits or proliferation of AI-driven firms. Those predictions are expressed by the SRA and its chief executive on institutional authority.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Authorisation is reported as of 6 May 2025; future benefits and wider adoption have no specified deadline and are qualified by safeguards and responsible use.
pts.d: The release reports an accomplished authorisation, but predicts future benefits without a timetable. Despite the description 'purely AI-based', Garfield is expressly not autonomous: each step requires client approval, with supervision and monitoring and greater oversight during the initial launch phase. The system cannot propose relevant case law, which the SRA identifies as a high-risk area. Named regulated solicitors retain responsibility for outputs and failures, and regulated firms must maintain minimum insurance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Immediate users are SMEs and law and other firms recovering debts; broader potential beneficiaries are people and small businesses with unmet legal needs.
pts.d: Garfield's stated market is small and medium sized businesses, alongside law and other firms, seeking unpaid-debt recovery assistance. The wider access claim concerns people and small businesses struggling to obtain legal services, not demonstrated enterprise savings. Clients retain step-by-step approval, while named solicitors remain accountable for system outputs. The SRA commits to monitoring the emerging model to protect consumers while enabling potential benefits.
